prompt: The bookshop's `pom.xml` gains the `org.postgresql:postgresql` dependency. What does that jar give the application?
hint: Think about what still has to be running before the application starts.

choices.text: A copy of PostgreSQL that starts inside the application's own JVM
choices.why: That is an embedded database, like H2. PostgreSQL is a separate server process; the jar contains none of it.

choices.text: The driver, which speaks PostgreSQL's protocol to a server running elsewhere
choices.why: Right. The jar is a client. A server must already be listening, on this machine or another, before the bookshop can connect.

choices.text: The PostgreSQL server, which Maven installs on the machine during the build
choices.why: Maven only puts jars on a class path. Installing a server is `apt`'s job, which is why the lesson installs one first.

choices.text: The SQL language, which the JDK cannot read without an extra library
choices.why: Java never reads SQL at all: it sends the text to the server, and the server parses it.

prompt: You took the online path: a hosted PostgreSQL with its own address, user and password. What do you change in the bookshop so it connects there?
hint: Which file names where the database is?

choices.text: The driver dependency, since a hosted server speaks another protocol
choices.why: A hosted PostgreSQL is still PostgreSQL, and the same driver talks to it. Only the address and the credentials differ.

choices.text: Nothing: Spring Boot finds a hosted database on the network by itself
choices.why: Boot discovers nothing on a network. It connects to exactly the URL it is given, and `localhost` is not the hosted server.

choices.text: The `spring.datasource` URL, user and password in `application.properties`
choices.why: Right. Those three lines are where the server is and who logs in. The service's page gives the values, usually with an encryption option in the URL.

choices.text: The SQL in `schema.sql`, because a hosted server uses a different dialect
choices.why: The dialect is PostgreSQL's wherever the server runs. The script does not change.

prompt: Right after installing, `psql` answers `FATAL:  role "ana" does not exist`. What does that tell you?
hint: The word FATAL comes from the server.

choices.text: PostgreSQL did not install, so there is nothing to connect to
choices.why: A server that is not running answers nothing at all, and psql says so differently. A FATAL line is the server refusing you, so it is running.

choices.text: The password for `ana` is wrong
choices.why: No password was asked. Over the local socket the server checks who you are on the computer, and the problem is that it has no such database user.

choices.text: The server is up and has no database user called `ana`
choices.why: Right. Database users, called roles, are a list of the server's own, separate from the machine's users. The installer creates only `postgres`.

choices.text: The machine has no Linux user called `ana`
choices.why: You are logged in as `ana`, so that user exists. The missing one is the server's role of that name.

prompt: `psql -U bookshop bookshop` fails with `Peer authentication failed`, yet `psql postgresql://bookshop:bookshop@localhost:5432/bookshop` gets in. Why the difference?
hint: The two commands reach the server by different doors.

choices.text: The role was created without `LOGIN`, which only TCP connections ignore
choices.why: Without `LOGIN` both would be refused. The URL version got in, so the role can log in.

choices.text: They use different doors: the socket checks by peer, TCP by password
choices.why: Right. Over the socket the server compares the computer's user, `ana`, with `bookshop`; over TCP it asks for the password. Ubuntu's `pg_hba.conf` uses peer for the socket and a password for `localhost`. JDBC always connects over TCP, so the password rule is the one the bookshop meets.

choices.text: `-U` is not supported by PostgreSQL 16, and a URL is the only way to name a user
choices.why: `-U` works; the refusal came from the server, after it read the user name.

choices.text: The password `bookshop` is wrong for the socket and right for TCP
choices.why: No password was asked on the socket at all. Peer authentication never looks at one.

prompt: Put the setup of the bookshop's database in the order it has to happen.
hint: Each step needs the one before it to exist.
items: Create the role bookshop, with LOGIN and a password
Create the database bookshop, owned by that role
Connect as bookshop over localhost and run a SELECT
trap: createdb -O bookshop names an owner, so the role has to exist before the database does.

prompt: Inserting The Time Machine a second time, with the same ISBN, is refused. Which part of the table's definition refuses it?
hint: The new row would have had a new `id`.

choices.text: `PRIMARY KEY` on `id`, because the row is a duplicate
choices.why: The second row would get a fresh `id` from the sequence, so the primary key never sees a repeat. It only guards `id`.

choices.text: `UNIQUE` on `isbn`
choices.why: Right. The error names the constraint `book_isbn_key`, which PostgreSQL made from `UNIQUE`, and the detail names the ISBN that already exists.

choices.text: `NOT NULL` on `title`
choices.why: The title was given. `NOT NULL` refuses a missing value, not a repeated one.

choices.text: `CHECK (price_cents >= 0)`
choices.why: 2950 passes that check. The CHECK is what refused Frankenstein's -1.

prompt: The column type that makes PostgreSQL number the rows itself, 1, 2, 3, from a sequence of its own, is `___`.
hint: It is the type of `id` in the CREATE TABLE.

prompt: Which of these rows does the `book` table refuse? Choose all that apply.
hint: Read the four constraints in the CREATE TABLE, one per column that has one.

choices.text: A book priced at -100 cents
choices.why: Right: `CHECK (price_cents >= 0)` refuses it.

choices.text: A book whose ISBN is already in the table
choices.why: Right: `UNIQUE` on `isbn` refuses it.

choices.text: A book with no title
choices.why: Right: `title` is `NOT NULL`, and a missing value is a null.

choices.text: A third book by H. G. Wells
choices.why: Nothing constrains `author`. Many books by one author is the normal case.

choices.text: A second book called Dom Casmurro, with a different ISBN
choices.why: Titles are not unique, and should not be: two editions share a title and differ in ISBN.

prompt: `java Jdbc.java 'H. G. Wells'`, run without `-cp`, fails with `No suitable driver found for jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/bookshop`. What is missing?
hint: `DriverManager` asks every driver it can see.

choices.text: The PostgreSQL driver jar on the class path
choices.why: Right. Without it no driver claims a `jdbc:postgresql:` URL, and `DriverManager` gives up before any network traffic.

choices.text: A running server on port 5432
choices.why: A missing server gives a different message, about a refused connection. This one is raised before anything is sent.

choices.text: A correctly spelt URL
choices.why: The URL is the one that works with `-cp`. Nothing claimed it because nothing able to was loaded.

choices.text: `Class.forName("org.postgresql.Driver")` at the start of `main`
choices.why: That line was needed before JDBC 4. Today a driver jar registers itself when it is on the class path, and without the jar the line would fail too.

prompt: `Jdbc.java 'Mary Shelley'` runs while no book by her is in the table. What happens?
hint: Where does a `ResultSet` start?

choices.text: `executeQuery` throws an `SQLException`, because the query found nothing
choices.why: No rows is a perfectly good answer to a query. JDBC reports it as an empty result, not as an error.

choices.text: `rows` is `null`, and the `while` throws a `NullPointerException`
choices.why: `executeQuery` always returns a `ResultSet`. An empty one is still an object.

choices.text: The first `next()` answers `false`, the loop body never runs, and nothing is printed
choices.why: Right. The cursor starts before the first row; with no rows there is nowhere to move to. The program exits normally with no output.

choices.text: `getLong("id")` throws, because there is no current row to read
choices.why: It would, if it were reached. The loop condition stops the program before any getter runs.

prompt: Match each JDBC type in `Jdbc.java` to what it is.
hint: Follow the program from the top: open, prepare, run, read.

pairs.right: finds the driver that accepts the URL and opens a connection
one logged-in session with the server
SQL with ? placeholders, whose values are set separately
a cursor over the rows a query returned

right_distractors: a pool that lends out connections that are already open

prompt: Inside the `while` loop of `Jdbc.java`, `getInt("price_cents")` throws an `SQLException`. Nothing in the program catches it. What happens to the connection?
hint: What does try-with-resources promise about the way out?

choices.text: It stays open until the garbage collector finds the `Connection` object
choices.why: That was the risk before try-with-resources, and it is how a server runs out of connections. The `try` closes it on any exit.

choices.text: It is closed only if a `catch` block is added for the `SQLException`
choices.why: A `catch` is not needed for closing. The resources close whether the block ends normally or by an exception, and then the exception carries on.

choices.text: It is closed first, so that the result set and the statement can close cleanly after it
choices.why: The order is the reverse of opening: the result set first, the statement next, the connection last.

choices.text: All three close, innermost first, then the exception leaves `main`
choices.why: Right. The result set, then the statement, then the connection. Each `try` closes what it opened, innermost first, before the exception propagates. The program then ends with the stack trace.

prompt: `Unsafe.java "Flannery O'Connor"` fails with a syntax error, while `Jdbc.java` with the same name finds Wise Blood. What went wrong in `Unsafe.java`?
hint: Read the SQL that `Unsafe.java` printed before it failed.

choices.text: PostgreSQL cannot store an apostrophe in a `text` column
choices.why: It stored one: Wise Blood is in the table, and `Jdbc.java` read the name back.

choices.text: Java needs the apostrophe escaped as `\'` inside the `String`
choices.why: The Java string is fine; the program compiled and printed it. The problem is what the text means as SQL.

choices.text: The apostrophe closed the quoted text, and the rest became SQL
choices.why: Right. Pasted into the statement, the input stopped being a value and became SQL. Here the driver, reading that SQL, found a string that never ends.

choices.text: The driver rejects any character outside ASCII before sending the query
choices.why: An apostrophe is ASCII. The driver did stop the query, but because its own reading of the SQL found a quoted string with no end.

prompt: A colleague fixes `Unsafe.java` by doubling every apostrophe in the input before concatenating, which is valid SQL. Why is a `PreparedStatement` still the fix to keep?
hint: Count the places that have to remember the rule.

choices.text: Doubling apostrophes is not accepted by PostgreSQL
choices.why: It is accepted: the lesson inserts `'Flannery O''Connor'` exactly that way, by hand.

choices.text: The value never enters the SQL text, so there is nothing to escape
choices.why: Right. Escaping has to be correct in every query that builds text, for every type of value. A parameter removes the question instead of answering it.

choices.text: A prepared statement is faster, and speed is the reason to prefer it
choices.why: It can be, when a statement is reused, but that is a side effect. The reason in this lesson is that data cannot become SQL.

choices.text: Doubling apostrophes would corrupt every ISBN in the catalogue
choices.why: An ISBN has no apostrophe, so doubling changes nothing in it. The objection is not about damage to the data.

prompt: A search screen lets the user pick the column to sort by. Which part of `SELECT ... FROM book WHERE author = ? ORDER BY title` can a `?` stand for?
hint: A parameter is sent as a value.

choices.text: The table name, `book`
choices.why: A table name is part of the statement the server plans, so it cannot arrive later as a value. Names have to be in the SQL text.

choices.text: The column after `ORDER BY`, as the user chose it
choices.why: Same reason: a column name is a name. To let a user choose, map their choice to one of a fixed list of names written in the code.

choices.text: The value compared with `author`
choices.why: Right. That is the only one of the four that is data. Everything else shapes the statement and must be written in it.

choices.text: The keyword `WHERE`
choices.why: A keyword is the statement's grammar. A parameter only fills a place where a value goes.

prompt: Why does `application.properties` set `spring.sql.init.mode=always`?
hint: What does Boot do with `schema.sql` by default?

choices.text: To drop the tables and create them again on every start
choices.why: Nothing in the scripts drops anything: `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` leaves an existing table alone.

choices.text: Boot runs them alone only for an embedded database
choices.why: Right. PostgreSQL is not embedded, and for a real server the default is to run nothing, and this property asks for the scripts every time.

choices.text: To switch on JDBC, which is off until a property enables it
choices.why: The starter on the class path is what brings JDBC in. This property is only about the two scripts.

choices.text: To have Flyway apply the scripts as migrations
choices.why: There is no Flyway yet. Lesson 13 brings it, and removes these two scripts when it does.

prompt: `data.sql` runs on every start of the bookshop. Why does the catalogue not gain three more copies of the same books each time?
hint: Read the last line of `data.sql`, and the column it names.

choices.text: Boot records which scripts it has already run and skips them
choices.why: Boot keeps no record; that history is what Flyway adds in lesson 13. The script really does run every time.

choices.text: `schema.sql` drops the table first, so the three rows start again from nothing
choices.why: It does not drop anything, and the book added through the API survives the restart, which a drop would have removed.

choices.text: `ON CONFLICT (isbn) DO NOTHING` skips the existing ISBNs
choices.why: Right. The insert is attempted every time, and each row that would break the constraint is quietly left out.

choices.text: `JdbcClient` ignores a duplicate row when it reads the table
choices.why: The rows would really be in the table. Reading cannot undo a write; the duplicates are prevented at the insert.

prompt: `query(Book.class)` fills the record `Book(long id, String isbn, String title, String author, int priceCents)` from the columns `id, isbn, title, author, price_cents`. How does `priceCents` get its value?
hint: `Book` is a record, so it has one constructor.

choices.text: By position: the fifth column goes to the fifth component
choices.why: The mapping is by name. Reordering the columns in the `SELECT` would not move the values.

choices.text: From a `@Column("price_cents")` annotation that the record needs
choices.why: There is no annotation on `Book`. Mapping by annotation is JPA's way, in lesson 10.

choices.text: By name: each constructor parameter is matched to a column
choices.why: Right. Spring calls the record's constructor, and matches each constructor parameter to a column, treating an underscore and the next capital letter as the same name.

choices.text: Jackson turns the row into JSON and reads it back into the record
choices.why: Jackson is the web layer's, for the HTTP body. Rows never become JSON on their way into a record.

prompt: Why does the `INSERT` in `JdbcBookRepository.save` end with `RETURNING id`?
hint: Who chooses the new book's id?

choices.text: Because the database generates the id, and this hands it back in the same statement
choices.why: Right. `bigserial` takes the next number from a sequence, which only the server knows. `RETURNING` returns it, and `withId` puts it in the record.

choices.text: To confirm the insert succeeded; without it a failure would be silent
choices.why: A failed insert throws an exception either way. `RETURNING` is about getting a value back, not about errors.

choices.text: Because `JdbcClient` cannot run an `INSERT` without a result to read
choices.why: `JdbcClient` has `update()` for statements that return nothing. This one uses `query` because it does return something.

choices.text: To send the id that `BookService` chose to the database
choices.why: The service passes 0, and the `INSERT` names no `id` column at all. The value comes from the server.

prompt: In `save`, the named placeholders `:isbn`, `:title`, `:author` and `:priceCents` are filled from the record's accessors by the call `.___(book)`.
hint: It is the line between the SQL text and `.query(Long.class)`.

prompt: With the bookshop running and nobody using it, `pg_stat_activity` counted the connections the pool held open. How many were there?
hint: HikariCP's default size, unchanged by any property in this lesson.

prompt: Match each message the bookshop or `Jdbc.java` printed to what it means.
hint: Ask how far each attempt got: the class path, the network, the login, the database.

pairs.left: No suitable driver found for jdbc:postgresql://…
pairs.right: no driver on the class path accepts the URL
nothing is listening on that host and port

pairs.left: FATAL: password authentication failed for user "bookshp"
pairs.right: the login was refused, and only the server's log says why
the login worked, and the database is missing

right_distractors: the table book has not been created yet

prompt: A colleague's copy of the bookshop fails with `password authentication failed for user "bookshop"`. They have checked the password three times against the one they set with `CREATE ROLE`. What is the most useful next step?
hint: The client is told less than the server knows.

choices.text: Reset the role's password and try again
choices.why: If the password really matches, resetting changes nothing. The same message also covers a role that does not exist, and a reset would hide that.

choices.text: Raise HikariCP's connection timeout, since the server may be slow to answer
choices.why: A slow server gives a timeout, not a FATAL line. This answer came back quickly and definitely.

choices.text: Read the server's log, whose DETAIL line says whether the role exists
choices.why: Right. The server tells the client only that the login failed, so that strangers cannot test which names exist. The log names the real cause, for example a role spelt differently.

choices.text: Change `localhost` to `127.0.0.1` in the URL
choices.why: Both reach the same TCP door and the same password rule. The server answered, so the address is not the problem.

prompt: A `POST /books` with a new ISBN reaches the bookshop. Put what happens in order.
hint: The service checks before it saves, and the connection is only borrowed.
items: BookService asks findByIsbn whether the ISBN is taken
JdbcClient borrows a connection from the pool for the INSERT
PostgreSQL takes the next id from the sequence and returns it
The connection goes back to the pool
The controller answers 201 with a Location naming the new id
trap: The connection is returned before the response is written: it is borrowed for the statement, not for the request.

prompt: Two `POST /books` requests with the same new ISBN arrive at the same instant. Both run `findByIsbn` before either has inserted, so both see nothing. What stops the catalogue from holding two rows with that ISBN?
hint: Which rule holds whatever program does the writing?

choices.text: `BookService`'s check, because it runs before every `save`
choices.why: It ran, twice, and both times truthfully found nothing. A check and a later insert leave a gap that two requests can both pass through.

choices.text: The pool, which gives out one connection at a time so the requests cannot overlap
choices.why: The pool held ten connections, so two requests run side by side on two of them.

choices.text: `ON CONFLICT (isbn) DO NOTHING`, which skips the second row
choices.why: That clause is in `data.sql` only. The repository's `INSERT` has none, so its second insert is refused rather than skipped.

choices.text: The `UNIQUE` constraint on `isbn`, in the database
choices.why: Right. The database refuses the second `INSERT`, and it fails with an exception. The table is the last line, and it holds. The second request gets an error rather than a 409, which is what lesson 14 deals with.

prompt: A teammate writes `connection.prepareStatement(String.format("SELECT id, title FROM book WHERE author = '%s'", author))` and says it is safe because it uses a prepared statement. Is it?
hint: What reaches the server as SQL text?

choices.text: Yes: `prepareStatement` escapes whatever text it is given, quotes included
choices.why: It escapes nothing in the SQL text. It only keeps apart the values set through `?`, and there are none here.

choices.text: No: the name is in the SQL text before `prepareStatement` sees it
choices.why: Right. It is exactly `Unsafe.java`. The protection is the placeholder and the separate value. Built with `String.format`, the statement is concatenation with a different method name.

choices.text: Yes, as long as the `author` column is declared with the type `text`
choices.why: The column type does not matter. Flannery O'Connor breaks this statement in the same way as `Unsafe.java`.

choices.text: No, because `String.format` cannot be used with JDBC at all
choices.why: It can build any string, and that string is the problem. Formatting is fine for text that is not SQL.
